title: Elbert County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Elbert County wells have a median depth of 341 ft and median yield of 12 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply on your property.
h1: Understanding water wells in Elbert County, Colorado
intro_html: Elbert County sits over the Denver Basin, so most wells tap sedimentary bedrock aquifers instead of shallow river gravels. That gives you fairly predictable depths and decent yields, but also real drilling costs you need to budget for. Here’s how existing wells across the county are actually performing, and what that usually means for a new build or land purchase.

sections.heading: How deep Elbert County wells usually go
sections.html:
Across Elbert County, the median well depth is 341 feet, with the middle half between 225 and 450 feet. About 51% of wells are in the 300–600 foot range, and another 25% are 100–300 feet. Only 12% are shallower than 100 feet, and another 12% go deeper than 600 feet. The deepest on record in the county is 3,880 feet, but that’s an outlier.

In practice, most bids here will be based on something in the 300–450 foot range unless nearby wells or a specific aquifer target say otherwise. Because this is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, depth is driven more by which aquifer you’re in and your elevation than by a shallow water table.

sections.heading: Well yield in Elbert County: how much water is normal
sections.html:
Production here is generally solid. The county-wide median yield is 12 gpm, and the middle half of wells fall between 10 and 14 gpm. Only 5% of wells report between 1–5 gpm, and none report under 1 gpm. About 74% of wells are in the 5–15 gpm band, and 22% report 15+ gpm.

For a typical exempt domestic well, anything over 5 gpm is usually workable with storage. With so many wells at or above 10 gpm, most single-family homes and small stock uses are well covered from a supply standpoint. The key is still to look at individual nearby permits, especially around places like Elizabeth, Kiowa, or Elbert, to see how your specific area compares.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels in Elbert County have a median of 165 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 97 and 240 feet. That means on a typical 341-foot well, about half the hole is water column when it’s not being pumped.

Looking over time, median static levels by decade deepened from about 30 feet in the 1950s to 222 feet in the 1990s, then came up somewhat to 160 feet in the 2010s, and are around 185 feet in the 2020s. That history suggests the table has generally dropped from the earliest days but has moved around rather than steadily crashing. Still, you should assume your pump will sit well below 200 feet in many parts of the county.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and how active it is
sections.html:
Elbert County has a long drilling history, with 17,502 wells in the state records and 10,074 recorded as constructed. Permits ramped up sharply starting in the 1970s: 1,528 that decade, then 1,973 in the 1980s, and a peak of 4,138 in the 1990s. The 2000s saw 3,479 permits, the 2010s had 2,240, and there are already 1,404 in the 2020s, with the newest permit in 2026.

The county is heavily developed on wells, especially for domestic use. Major drillers on record include Hamacher Well Works Inc with 3,994 wells, Parker Drilling/Pump Service Inc. with 1,395, and Hier Drilling Co Inc with 1,163. That depth of experience helps keep designs consistent across the Denver Basin aquifers.

sections.heading: Aquifers and geology under Elbert County
sections.html:
On paper, this is Denver Basin country. About 97% of wells are completed in Denver Basin aquifers. Named aquifers on permits include the Upper Dawson with 3,389 wells and the Denver aquifer with 2,569 wells, along with about 5,376 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock settings.

These sedimentary formations tend to give more predictable drilling than hard crystalline rock, but yields and depths still vary by location and target aquifer. Because most domestic wells (78% of use) are on these same systems, checking which aquifer your neighbors are in and how deep they went is the best way to estimate your own depth.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Elbert County
sections.html:
Drilling in Elbert County’s Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock typically runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the county median depth of 341 feet, that puts the drilled hole itself in the $17,000–$23,900 range. By the time you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished median-depth well usually lands between about $23,000 and $35,900.

If you end up closer to 450 feet instead of 225 feet, that’s a significant swing, so it’s worth pulling permits around Ponderosa Park, Elizabeth, Kiowa, Elbert, Simla, or Matheson to see what depths and aquifers are typical right around your parcel before you finalize budgets.

sections.heading: Risks and checks: water quality, low yield, and siting
sections.html:
There are 40 mapped PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 5 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, and 1 historic mine feature within about 10 miles in the wider area. That doesn’t mean your well is contaminated, but it does mean you should plan on lab testing for PFAS and common domestic parameters before relying on the water.

Low-yield or dry holes are less common here than in some mountain areas, based on the yield stats, but they’re never impossible. Also keep in mind most wells here are permitted for domestic/household use (78%), with 38% including stock and 9% irrigation, so you need to match your planned uses to the permit and to your septic layout and building envelope.

sections.heading: Practical advice for buying or building on Elbert County land
sections.html:
Before you buy, look up nearby well permits in Elbert County and note three things: depth, yield, and aquifer. With a county median depth of 341 feet and median yield of 12 gpm, you’re starting from a favorable baseline, but local pockets still vary.

Budget on the high side of the cost range if neighboring wells are deeper than 400 feet, and confirm there’s room on the lot to separate the well from future septic. Given the PFAS and cleanup sites in the region, plan on a comprehensive water test as part of closing or right after drilling. For irrigated livestock or lawn plans, double-check that the well use on the permit covers what you intend to do.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Elbert County, Colorado?
faq.a: Across all reported wells in Elbert County, the median total depth is about 341 feet, with the middle half between 225 and 450 feet. Roughly 51% of wells are 300–600 feet deep, 25% are 100–300 feet, and 12% go beyond 600 feet. Only about 12% of wells are shallower than 100 feet, so most new domestic wells will be planned in the few-hundred-foot range.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Elbert County?
faq.a: Reported wells in Elbert County show a median yield of 12 gpm, with the middle half running from 10 to 14 gpm. About 74% of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range, and 22% report 15+ gpm. Only 5% are in the 1–5 gpm band and none report under 1 gpm. That level of production is usually adequate for a single-family home and modest stock use, often with some storage.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Elbert County?
faq.a: In Elbert County’s Denver Basin bedrock, typical drilling rates run about $50–$70 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 341 feet, the borehole alone runs roughly $17,000–$23,900. Once you add a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a complete median-depth well commonly totals in the $23,000–$35,900 range. Deeper wells toward 450–600 feet increase those costs noticeably.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Elbert County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. In the broader area there are 40 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 1 historic mine feature mapped within about 10 miles. Many private wells still produce good water, but you should plan on a full lab test for PFAS and standard drinking-water parameters before using any Elbert County well as your household supply.

faq.q: Which aquifer do Elbert County wells use?
faq.a: Elbert County is mainly drilled into the Denver Basin aquifers, with about 97% of wells completed there. Named aquifers on permits include the Upper Dawson aquifer with 3,389 wells and the Denver aquifer with 2,569 wells, plus about 5,376 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Your exact aquifer will depend on location and well design, so check your permit and nearby well records.
